case_title: Shraddha Gupta v. State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_occupation: Household lady (as claimed by the appellant; not independently stated by the Court)
previous_criminal_record: Not stated (appellant's counsel contended she is not a habitual offender; no record described)
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (sibling; the appellant and the deceased were daughters of the same father, in a property dispute)
statutory_provisions: Gangsters Act, 1986 ss.2 and 3 (charged against appellant); underlying case Case Crime No. 337/2016 under IPC ss.147, 304, 504, 323, 506, 120-B
weapon: None mentioned (a car was used to ram the victim's scooty)
evidence_type: Call recordings between co-accused (investigation material); gang chart. The Court did not assess trial evidence.
aggravating_circumstances: Alleged: planned murder by an organised gang led by a mastermind for pecuniary gain; alleged order to kill the driver as he might give evidence
trial_court_outcome: Not stated for the appellant (no trial verdict against her in this judgment; Special Court took cognizance against eight co-accused)
high_court_outcome: Writ petition under s.482 CrPC dismissed and refusal to quash Gangsters Act proceedings upheld; review application also dismissed
neutral_facts: The victim was travelling on the rear seat of a scooty driven by her servant, returning from a district court in the evening. Near a temple, the victim and her driver saw a car with several persons parked nearby. The car followed the scooty and, near a village, rammed into it, and both the victim and the driver fell onto the road. The car then stopped near the driver, and a person in it shouted that the driver should also be killed because he might give evidence. The assailants fled when passers-by gathered. Passers-by helped the driver take the victim to a hospital, where she died. An autopsy was conducted that night. The victim's sister lodged a written report the next day, alleging prior enmity between the family and the accused. Investigation later relied on call recordings between co-accused, provided to the investigating officer by the complainant, which led to the identification of additional accused. Investigators found that the daughters of the victim's late father had been in prolonged litigation over the division of his immovable properties. The prosecution's case was that one accused was the leader of an organised gang who planned the killing for pecuniary gain, with other co-accused, including the later-added accused, joining in. A gang chart was prepared and a supplementary charge sheet was filed against the later-added accused.
offence_severity: Minimum 2 years and maximum 10 years imprisonment, plus fine of not less than Rs. 5,000 (Gangsters Act s.3(1), as quoted)
physical_harm: Death of the victim after the car rammed her scooty; the driver fell on the road (injuries not described)
number_of_offences: 2 charged (Gangsters Act ss.2 and 3) against the appellant; 0 finally upheld (no conviction; proceedings not quashed)
premeditation_planning: Not decided by the Court; planning and conspiracy were alleged by the prosecution/State
motive: alleged: pecuniary benefit from a long-running property dispute among the family members
key_evidence_accepted: None assessed; the Court relied on the allegations as presented and on the statutory definitions, not on trial evidence
trial_duration: offence: 23.05.2016; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 27.09.2019 (writ order), 10.11.2020 (review order); Supreme Court: 26.04.2022
legal_representation: Appellant: Divyesh Pratap Singh and others (Advs.); State of UP: Sanjay Kumar Tyagi and others; respondent no.4: Shuvodeep Roy and others
investigation_status: FIR registered 24.05.2016 (Case Crime 337/2016); charge sheet and supplementary charge sheet filed; Gangsters Act FIR registered 27.05.2019 against the appellant and two co-accused
procedural_irregularity: None noted by the Court (appellant alleged the gang chart was maliciously submitted)
appeal_history: Trial court: not stated for the appellant. High Court: writ petition under s.482 CrPC dismissed (27.09.2019); review dismissed (10.11.2020). Supreme Court: appeals dismissed.
prosecution_argument: The appellant is a member of the gang who took part in anti-social activity (conspiracy to murder for pecuniary gain), so she can be prosecuted under the Gangsters Act even on a single FIR; no bar like MCOCA or GCTOC applies.
defence_argument: A single FIR/charge sheet for one murder cannot make the appellant a gangster or gang member; she was not named in the FIR and was added later under s.173(8) CrPC; the allegations are not anti-social activities; Piyush Kantilal Mehta and the Gujarat High Court decision were relied on.
legal_principle_applied: A single offence/FIR/charge sheet suffices for prosecution under the Gangsters Act if the accused is a gang member who indulged in a s.2(b) anti-social activity by violence, threat, intimidation or coercion for undue advantage; statutory provisions are read as they are.
precedent_relied_upon: Piyush Kantilal Mehta v. Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad City, 1989 Supp (1) SCC 322; Karansinh Chetansinh Vaghela v. State of Gujarat, 2021 SCC OnLine Gujarat 1260 (both cited by the appellant and noted as referred to; the Court's reasoning rests on the statutory text)
